2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).

Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern / Not applicable at case level: Both selected municipalities (Indaial and Itapema) are tracked across the entire 2003–2009 study window and into the subsequent municipal electoral term, although longitudinal indicator completeness is asymmetric across cases (e.g., water/sewer coverage reported at 2001 and 2009 for Itapema via SNIS, versus a single cross-section from FURB 2010 for Indaial).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Major baseline structural confounders separate Indaial and Itapema—industrial textile economy vs. coastal seasonal tourism with floating summer population, population size (43,000 vs. 26,000), income/poverty and inequality, civil-society and river-basin institutional density, and political stability/ideology (PT participatory governance vs. impeached PFL mayor). While narratively described, the N=2 descriptive comparison cannot adjust for these confounders, and the authors note that socio-economic and ideological factors endogenously determined model choice.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-strong: Municipal governance regimes and regulatory exposures are concretely operationalized through primary legal and administrative instruments (Indaial Lei Municipal 3.218/2003, Lei 3.255/04, Convênio 001/04 with CASAN, CMSA and FUNSAM rules; Itapema Edital de Concorrência 003/03 and 004/03, court injunctions, 25-year concession terms, SMRC), with only minor citation/typographical slips (e.g., federal Lei 11.455/07 typo for 11.445/07 on PDF p. 4; court name imprecision in Note 19 on PDF p. 15).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Comparative operational, financial, and coverage figures rely on heterogeneous secondary sources and mismatched years ('os dados partem de bases diferentes', PDF p. 12; FURB 2010 vs. SNIS 2001/2009 and Andersen 2009; CASAN vs. FGV 2008 and municipal reports) without standardized accounting formulas or inflation adjustments; service-quality problems in Itapema are documented via local press complaints without symmetrical press-complaint quantification for Indaial; and embedded cells of Tables 1–3 are absent from the PDF text layer (though key figures are stated in prose).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Water supply and sanitation outcomes (network coverage, septic-tank share, R$/m³ water production cost, disconnection rate, tariff re-balancing, and social participation) are drawn from non-uniform institutional reports across different years without harmonized denominators, baseline-to-endline symmetry for both municipalities, or uncertainty/audit verification.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: No pre-specified protocol or systematic content-coding scheme governs the extraction of evidence from weekly local newspapers (2003–2009), monthly CMSA minutes (2004–2009), or grey administrative reports, creating risk of selective indicator and episode reporting across the two cases (e.g., 2% disconnection rate reported only for Indaial; water-shortage and sewage-leak press reports cited primarily for Itapema).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Purposive N=2 selection of contrasting post-CASAN municipal governance cases in Santa Catarina (Indaial shared management vs. Itapema privatization) involves strong baseline structural and political self-selection into each governance regime, and no explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria are stated for selecting auxiliary grey reports and local/regional media sources (e.g., Timbó's Jornal Médio Vale for Indaial).

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Paludo and Borba (2013) present a comparative institutional-historical case study of two post-CASAN municipal water supply and sanitation governance models implemented between 2003 and 2009 in Santa Catarina, Brazil: shared public-participatory management ('Gestão Compartilhada') in Indaial versus a 25-year private concession ('Gestão Privatizada') in Itapema. Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (as a structured non-validated judgment), the study demonstrates strong jurisdictional specificity, concrete operationalization of municipal legal-institutional regimes (statutes, council/fund structures, social tariffs, tender notices, and litigation), and rich political-institutional contextualization—including documenting institutional persistence after partisan alternation in both municipalities. However, methodological concerns are substantial regarding causal identification, confounding, and outcome measurement: with N=2 purposively selected municipalities, endogenous socio-economic and partisan selection into governance models (industrial economy and strong civil society in Indaial vs. seasonal coastal tourism and political turmoil in Itapema), unstandardized documentary/newspaper coding, and asymmetric secondary data bases ('os dados partem de bases diferentes') lacking baseline-to-endline parity across cases, descriptive differences in unit water cost (R$2.1 vs. R$2.7/m³) and coverage cannot be causally attributed to the legal management model alone.
raw_response.overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (strong institutional contextualization, jurisdictional specificity, and legal exposure definition; weak causal identification, confounding control, outcome harmonization, and coding transparency)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Comparative institutional and legal-historical case study (2003–2009) of two municipalities in Santa Catarina, Brazil, combining regulatory/statutory and litigation analysis, local weekly newspaper archives, municipal council minutes, and descriptive secondary administrative statistics
raw_response.where_found_summary: Methods and case-comparison design on PDF p. 7 ('Casos comparados') and PDF pp. 19–20 ('Resumo'/'Abstract'); regulatory and municipal legal-institutional frameworks on PDF pp. 4, 6–7, and 9–11 ('Marco regulatório e modelos de gestão', 'A situação do abastecimento...', 'Desenho dos dois modelos'); comparative socio-economic, financial, and coverage outcomes on PDF pp. 8–9, 11–14 ('Casos comparados', 'Análise e conclusões') and PDF pp. 14–18 ('Notas', 'Referências'). Note: all 20 pages of prose, footnotes, and references are fully readable in the text layer, though the interior cells of embedded Tables 1–3 are omitted from the extracted text (key values are reported in prose and Footnote 22).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study is a comparative institutional and legal-historical case study (N=2 municipalities, Indaial vs. Itapema, 2003–2009) relying on municipal statutes, concession bidding notices, court rulings, monthly council minutes, weekly newspaper archives, and descriptive secondary utility/municipal figures. It conducts no primary human-subject qualitative fieldwork (interviews, focus groups, ethnography) and no quantitative statistical/econometric or quasi-experimental estimation (precluding ROBINS-I, JBI Cross-Sectional/Cohort, and MMAT), making the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the most appropriate instrument.
